title: How to Negotiate a Salary Offer Over Email: 4 Polite Templates
meta_description: Learn how to negotiate a salary offer over email: 4 polite, copy-ready templates, how to research your number, timing rules and phrases to avoid.
quick_answer: To negotiate a salary offer over email, wait for the written offer and respond before you sign. Thank the employer, confirm your interest, then name one specific figure backed by public salary data for the same role, level and location. Put every request in that single email, allow one or two rounds at most, avoid ultimatums or invented offers, and get final terms in writing.
key_takeaways: Negotiate after the written offer arrives and before you sign. The employer has chosen you, and nothing is final yet.
Base your figure on at least three public sources (the posted range, government wage data and salary-sharing sites), matched on duties, seniority and location.
Put every request in one email. Send one counter, plus no more than one follow-up.
If base pay is fixed, ask for a signing bonus, a later start date, extra time off or an early pay review instead.
Never mention personal expenses, give ultimatums or make up a competing offer.
Get the final terms in an updated, signed offer letter before you resign from your current job.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for anyone who has just received a written job offer and wants to ask for better pay or terms by email without sounding pushy or putting the offer at risk.
intro: A written job offer opens a short window. The employer has chosen you, but nothing is signed yet. That's the moment to negotiate, and email suits it well: you can word your request carefully, check your numbers and keep a record of what was agreed. This guide shows you how to back up your salary figure with public data, how fast to reply and how many rounds of emails stay professional. It then gives you four copy-ready email templates and the phrases that can ruin an otherwise reasonable request. It covers new job offers only. If you want more pay from your current employer, see our separate guide on asking for a raise.

steps.name: Acknowledge the offer within one business day
steps.text: Thank the employer, say you're excited about the role, and ask for the full written details and the date they need your decision. Don't negotiate in this first reply. Its job is to give you time to review the offer properly.

steps.name: Get the complete package in writing
steps.text: Before you judge the offer, make sure you have the base salary, bonus structure, any equity (company shares), a benefits summary, paid time off, the remote or office policy, the start date and any conditions, such as background or reference checks.

steps.name: Research a fair range from public data
steps.text: Collect at least three data points: the range in the job ad, government wage data (such as the US BLS OEWS survey or the UK ONS ASHE survey) and salary-sharing websites. Match each one on duties, seniority and location, and compare total pay, not just base salary.

steps.name: Set your three numbers and your priorities
steps.text: Write down your walk-away point (the lowest you'd accept), your realistic target and your opening ask. Then list one or two non-salary requests, most important first, so you know what to ask for if base pay turns out to be fixed.

steps.name: Pick the template that fits your situation
steps.text: Use Template 1 for higher base pay, Template 2 for benefits or a signing bonus, Template 3 if you're in late-stage interviews elsewhere, and Template 4 to accept gracefully (or decline politely) if the answer is no.

steps.name: Send one counter email with everything in it
steps.text: Put every request in a single short email. Send it from your personal account, in the same email thread, during business hours. Give one evidence-based reason and a specific figure, and read the email aloud once to check the tone before you send it.

steps.name: Respond once, then decide
steps.text: When the employer replies, either accept or make one final, smaller request. After that second round, accept, accept with a future pay review, or decline politely.

steps.name: Get the final terms in writing before you resign
steps.text: Wait for an updated offer letter that includes everything you agreed. Check it line by line, then sign it. Only then give notice to your current employer.

sections.heading: How to research a fair salary range from public data
paragraphs: To research a fair salary range, gather at least three public data points for the same duties, seniority and location, then see where your offer falls among them. One source can be skewed, but three that roughly agree give you a range you can explain in a single sentence.

Start with the job ad. Pay transparency laws in several US states and cities, including Colorado, California, Washington and New York, require many employers to post a pay range. The EU Pay Transparency Directive requires member states to bring in similar rules for job applicants. If your ad listed a range, that's the employer's own pay band and your strongest reference point. The rules depend on your location and the company's size, so check the official government guidance for your area.

Next, check government wage data. In the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) survey shows wages at the 10th, 25th, 50th (median), 75th and 90th percentiles by occupation, state and metro area. In the UK, the Office for National Statistics' Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE) reports earnings by occupation and region. These sources are large and neutral. But they're broad and lag behind the current market, so use them to sanity-check the low and high ends rather than as an exact target.

Then add salary-sharing websites such as Glassdoor, Payscale, LinkedIn Salary and, for tech roles, Levels.fyi. They show pay at named companies, sometimes including bonus and equity. But people report these figures themselves, and niche roles may have only a handful of entries. Favour recent entries at the same level, not just the same job title.

Finally, compare duties and total pay rather than job titles. A 'Senior Analyst' at a 50-person startup and one at a global bank can be very different jobs. Match the roles on responsibilities such as team size, budget and scope, then weigh base salary, bonus, equity and benefits together.

Turn your research into three numbers: your walk-away point (the lowest you'd accept), your realistic target and your opening ask. Here's an example with illustrative figures. If the offer is $70,000, the advertised range was $65,000–$80,000 and your other sources cluster around $72,000–$78,000, you might set a walk-away of $70,000, a target of $76,000 and an opening ask of $78,000. Keep your opening ask within what your evidence supports.
bullets: Job ad range: the employer's own pay band. Also check its other ads for similar roles
Government wage data: BLS OEWS (US) or ONS ASHE (UK), by occupation and area
US Department of Labor H-1B visa data: the wages specific employers filed for sponsored roles, useful for larger companies
Salary-sharing sites: Glassdoor, Payscale, LinkedIn Salary, Levels.fyi. Check how many entries there are and how recent they are
Professional association surveys and specialist recruiters: useful for niche roles with little public data

sections.heading: How to negotiate a salary offer over email: timing and rounds
paragraphs: When you negotiate a salary offer over email, reply within one business day to acknowledge the offer, send your counter before the decision deadline, and plan on one main counter plus no more than one follow-up. That pace shows real interest without rushing your research.

Your first email is a thank-you and a request for details, not a negotiation. Ask for anything missing from the written offer, and ask when they need your decision. For example: 'Thank you so much for the offer. I'm excited about the role. Could you send the full benefits details and let me know when you need my decision? I'll get back to you by [date].' Asking for two to three business days to review the offer is normal.

Send your counter as one email with every request in it: base salary, signing bonus, start date and time off. Adding requests one at a time across several emails makes the negotiation feel like a fight, because the employer can never tell when you're done.

Plan on one or two rounds from your side. In round one, you send your full counter. When the employer replies, either accept or make one final, smaller request. For example, if they met you partway on base pay, you might ask for a modest signing bonus to close the gap. Going back a third time usually costs more goodwill than it gains.

If the recruiter phones instead of replying by email, take the call. Then send a written summary within a few hours: 'Thanks for the call. To confirm, we discussed…'. You don't have to agree to a number on the spot. 'Let me review that and come back to you tomorrow' is a complete, professional answer.

Send every message from your personal email account, never your current employer's. Reply in the same thread so the recruiter has the full history. State figures the same way the offer does (for example, annual base salary in the same currency) so nothing gets misread.
bullets: Day 0: reply within one business day and ask for the full details and the deadline
Days 1–3: do your research, set your three numbers and send one counter email during business hours
No reply after two to three business days: send one short, friendly check-in
After two rounds from your side: accept, accept with a future pay review, or decline
Before you resign: get a signed, updated offer letter and check any conditions, such as background or reference checks

sections.heading: Template 1: Asking for more base pay
paragraphs: To ask for more base pay, thank the employer, give one evidence-based reason and name a single figure. Use this template when the salary is the main problem and your research shows similar roles pay more.
Subject: Re: Offer for [Job Title] – [Your Name]

Hi [Name], thank you again for the offer for the [Job Title] role. After speaking with [hiring manager/team], I'm even more excited about [specific project or goal], and I'd really like to make this work.

Before I sign, I wanted to discuss the base salary. Based on public pay data for [role] in [location], including [the advertised range / BLS figures for this occupation], and my [X years of specific experience or a skill central to this role], I'd like to ask for a base salary of [$target].
If we can reach [$target], I'm ready to accept by [date]. Thank you for considering this, and I'm happy to have a quick call if that's easier.
Best regards, [Your Name]
bullets: Give one reason tied to the role's responsibilities or your proven skills, never your personal costs
Name one figure. If you give a range, make the bottom of it your real target, because the employer can reasonably pick the low end
Only include the 'ready to accept' line if you would really sign at that number
Mention your sources in a short phrase rather than attaching a spreadsheet, and share more if they ask

sections.heading: Template 2: Negotiating benefits or a signing bonus
paragraphs: To negotiate benefits or a signing bonus, accept the base salary as set and ask for two or three specific extras. This works when base pay is fixed or already fair, but you're giving up a bonus, need a later start date or face moving costs. One-off and non-salary items can be easier to approve because they often don't change the company's pay bands.
Subject: Re: Offer for [Job Title] – [Your Name]
Hi [Name], thank you for the offer and for walking me through the full package. I'm excited to join [Company], and I understand the base salary for this level is set at [$amount].

I'd like to ask about flexibility in two areas. First, a one-time signing bonus of [$amount]. By leaving in [month], I'll give up [my annual bonus / shares that haven't vested yet] at my current employer, and this would help make up for it. Second, [a start date of (date) / (X) additional days of paid time off / a formal pay review at six months].
If these can work, I'd be glad to accept by [date]. Thanks so much for looking into it.
Best regards, [Your Name]
bullets: Often negotiable: signing bonus, start date, extra paid time off, remote or hybrid days, help with moving costs, a training budget, job title, an early pay review
Usually set for the whole company and hard to change: health plan options and retirement plan contributions
Stick to two or three requests and put the most important one first
Read the signing bonus terms carefully. Some require you to pay it back if you leave within a set period

sections.heading: Template 3: Countering when you have competing interviews
paragraphs: To counter when you have competing interviews, say honestly where the other processes stand and ask for a better offer, more time, or both. Never suggest you have an offer you don't.
Subject: Re: Offer for [Job Title] – [Your Name]
Hi [Name], thank you for the offer for the [Job Title] role. [Company] is [my first choice / one of my top choices], and I'd love to find a way to say yes.

To be transparent, I'm also in final-round interviews with [another company / two other companies] and expect to hear back by [date]. I'd much rather commit to [Company] now. A base salary of [$target], in line with what similar roles in [location] pay according to [source], would let me do that. If that isn't possible yet, could we extend my decision deadline to [date]?
I'm happy to talk this through by phone. Thank you for your flexibility.
Best regards, [Your Name]

If you already have a written offer from another employer, you can be more direct: 'I've received a written offer with a base salary of [$amount]. I'd prefer to join [Company]. Is there any flexibility to get closer to that figure?' Only say this if it's true, and expect to be asked for details.
bullets: Only say 'first choice' if it's true. 'One of my top choices' is honest if you're unsure
You don't have to name the other companies
Never make up or inflate an offer. If a bluff is discovered, it can cost you this offer and your reputation
If they extend your deadline, give your answer by that date even if the other interviews are delayed

sections.heading: Template 4: Accepting gracefully if the answer is no
paragraphs: If the answer is no and you still want the job, accept warmly in writing and confirm the final terms. If it matters to you, ask for a future pay review instead of reopening the negotiation. A gracious acceptance gets your relationship with your new employer off to a good start.
Subject: Re: Offer for [Job Title] – Acceptance

Hi [Name], thank you for checking on this and for being so open about where things stand. I understand, and I'm happy to accept the offer as written: [Job Title], base salary of [$amount], starting [date].

I'd appreciate the chance to revisit my pay after my first [six months / review cycle], once I've had time to deliver results. If that's possible, could it be noted in my offer letter or onboarding plan?
Please let me know the next steps for signing. I'm looking forward to getting started with the team.
Best regards, [Your Name]

If the gap is too large and you decide to decline, keep the email short and warm. Thank them for their time, say the package isn't the right fit for you right now, and offer to stay in touch. Don't use a decline as a bargaining tactic unless you're ready for them to accept it.
bullets: Repeat the agreed terms so there's a written record
Leave out any sign of disappointment, such as 'I guess' or 'I suppose'
Keep the pay review request to one line, or leave it out
Sign the final offer letter promptly once it arrives

sections.heading: What never to write in a salary negotiation email
paragraphs: Never write anything that bases your request on personal need, pressures the employer, or that you couldn't back up if asked. Those lines turn a routine negotiation into a question of trust.

You don't need to share your current salary in a negotiation email. Many US states and cities restrict employers from asking about your pay history. Even where they can ask, a counter based on what the new role pays in the market is stronger than one based on what you earn now. Check the rules for your location if you're unsure.
bullets: 'I need more because of my rent / loans / childcare costs.' Instead, base your request on the role's responsibilities and market data.
'This offer is a lowball' or 'frankly insulting.' Instead, write: 'I was hoping for something closer to [$X] based on…'
'Sorry to be difficult, I know this is a huge ask…' Instead, state your request plainly and thank them.
'I deserve…' Instead, point to specific evidence: your experience, results and salary data.
'I have another offer at [$X]' when you don't. Instead, describe your real situation, as in Template 3.
'Give me an answer by tomorrow or I'll go elsewhere.' Instead, ask about their timeline and share yours.
Copying in the hiring manager or a senior executive to go around the recruiter. Reply to whoever sent the offer.
Any new request after you've accepted. Once you say yes, the negotiation is over.

recommendations.best_for: Checking the tone of your counter email so it sounds confident rather than apologetic or blunt, and catching typos in a message the employer will read closely. Features and plans change, so confirm current details on Grammarly's website.
recommendations.not_for: Deciding what to ask for, because it can't replace salary research. Also not for anyone who'd rather not have offer details processed by an outside tool. Review your privacy settings and the vendor's current data policy first.

recommendations.best_for: Keeping track of several offers or interview processes at once, with your research sources, offer details, deadlines and email drafts on one comparison page.
recommendations.not_for: Someone weighing a single offer, because a simple note or spreadsheet does the job without any setup. Also, don't put job search details in a workspace your current employer manages.

faq.question: Is it OK to negotiate a job offer over email?
faq.answer: Yes. Email is a normal, professional way to negotiate a job offer. It gives you time to word your request carefully and leaves a written record of what was agreed. If the recruiter prefers to call, take the call and then send a short written summary afterwards.

faq.question: How much more should I ask for when negotiating a salary offer?
faq.answer: No single percentage fits every role. Ask for a specific figure near the top of the range your public salary research supports for the same duties, seniority and location, and make sure it's a number you'd be happy to accept. If the offer is already at the top of the advertised range, ask for things other than salary instead.

faq.question: Can a company withdraw a job offer because I tried to negotiate?
faq.answer: It can happen, because in many places an employer can withdraw an offer before you accept it. A polite, specific request backed by research is widely treated as a normal part of hiring, and the risk goes up mainly with ultimatums, aggressive language, bluffing or many rounds of requests. If you're worried about your rights in a specific situation, check your local employment law or speak to a qualified adviser.

faq.question: How long should I take to respond to a job offer email?
faq.answer: Reply within one business day to confirm you've received the offer, and ask when the employer needs your decision. Taking two to three business days to review the full package is a normal request. If the deadline is very short, it's reasonable to politely ask for a little more time.

faq.question: What should I do if the employer says the salary is non-negotiable?
faq.answer: Accept that the base salary is fixed and ask whether there's flexibility elsewhere, such as a signing bonus, start date, paid time off, remote days or an early pay review (Template 2). If nothing can change, decide whether the offer still works for you, then accept gracefully or decline politely.

faq.question: Should I tell the employer my current salary?
faq.answer: You don't have to share it, and many US states and cities restrict employers from asking about your pay history. A counter based on what the new role pays in the market is usually stronger than one based on what you earn now. If an employer asks, check the rules where you live and steer the conversation back to the role's pay range.

conclusion: Negotiating a salary offer over email comes down to three things: a figure based on public data, one well-organised message, and a tone that makes it easy for the employer to say yes. Pick the template that fits your situation, fill in your details, read it aloud once to check the tone and send it during business hours. Whatever the answer, get the outcome confirmed in an updated offer letter before you resign. If you want more pay from your current employer instead, see our separate guide on asking for a raise.
